verdicts.title: Upper bound on distance in the pants complex
verdicts.abstract_excerpt: The purpose of this paper is to establish an upper bound on the distance between two pants decompositions in the pants complex for a closed surface of genus g >= 2. This is done by use of graph theory. First distance is found in the pants graph modulo the action of the mapping class group, and then between pants decompositions within an orbit of this action.
verdicts.judge_reasoning: The abstract concerns distance bounds in the pants complex for closed surfaces of genus g >= 2, a topology/geometric group theory topic, which has no interaction with quasi-quadratic forms, Tseitin formulas, or proof entropy.

verdicts.title: An upper bound conjecture for the Yokota invariant
verdicts.abstract_excerpt: We conjecture an upper bound on the growth of the Yokota invariant of polyhedral graphs, extending a previous result on the growth of the $6j$-symbol. Using Barrett's Fourier transform we are able to prove this conjecture in a large family of examples. As a consequence of this result, we prove the Turaev-Viro Volume Conjecture for a new infinite family of hyperbolic manifolds.
verdicts.judge_reasoning: The abstract concerns the Yokota invariant of polyhedral graphs, 6j-symbols, and the Turaev-Viro Volume Conjecture for hyperbolic manifolds—quantum topology, not proof complexity, Tseitin formulas, or quasi-quadratic forms over F_2.

verdicts.title: A Sharper Upper Bound for the Separating Words Problem
verdicts.abstract_excerpt: We show that for any two distinct words $ s_1, s_2 $ over an arbitrary alphabets, there exists a deterministic finite automaton with $ O(\log^2 n) $ states that accepts $ s_1 $ and rejects $ s_2 $. This improves the previous upper bound of $O(n^{1/3}\log^7 n)$
verdicts.judge_reasoning: The abstract concerns DFA state complexity for the separating words problem ('deterministic finite automaton with O(log^2 n) states that accepts s_1 and rejects s_2'), which has no interaction with quasi-quadratic forms, Tseitin formulas, or cumulative proof entropy.
